chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ibn Isa, from Ibn Fadhal, from Abdullah ibn Bukayr and Thal'abah ibn Maymun and Ali ibn Uqba, from Zurara, from Abdul Malik, who said:

A discussion occurred between Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and the children of Al-Hasan (peace be upon him). That reached me, so I entered upon Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and went to speak, but he said to me, 'Hush! Do not interfere in what is between us. For our example and the example of the sons of our uncle is like the example of a man who was among the Children of Israel. He had two daughters, so he married one of them to a farmer and married the other to a potter.'

Then he visited them both. He began with the wife of the farmer and said to her, 'What is your condition?' She said, 'My husband has planted much crop. If Allah sends rain from the sky, we will be in the best condition of the Children of Israel.' Then he proceeded to the wife of the potter and said to her, 'What is your condition?' She said, 'My husband has made much pottery. If Allah withholds rain from the sky, we will be in the best condition of the Children of Israel.' So he returned, saying, 'O Allah, You are for them both,' and so it is with us.

key_terms.اللَّهُمَّ أَنْتَ لَهُمَا: O Allah, You are for them both

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of the parable of the farmer and the potter in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) employs the parable of a farmer and a potter to illustrate the divine wisdom behind the fluctuating fortunes of the Ahl al-Bayt and their kin, emphasizing that their status is contingent upon Allah's decree rather than human interference. This narrative underscores the Shia concept of *taqdir* (divine decree), where both ease and hardship serve as tests of patience and gratitude, ultimately affirming that all matters rest solely with God.
